<explanation>
Based on the file structure and README, UX Remote LAB is a full-stack web application for conducting usability tests and heuristic evaluations. It uses a Vue.js frontend with Vuetify, serverless backend functions hosted on Firebase (with additional Python functions for heuristic weight calculations), and integrates tightly with Firebase services such as Firestore and Authentication. Here’s how to sketch a detailed system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Major Components:
   • Client/Frontend: Represent the user-facing web application built using Vue.js (in the src folder). Inside the frontend, include the Vue components, views (including admin, public, and superAdmin pages), the router (managed via the src/router folder), Vuex state management (from the src/store), and assets such as faqs videos and landing images.
   • API/Backend (Firebase Functions): Show the cloud functions hosted in the functions folder. This is the serverless backend logic that manages authentication, database calls, heuristic evaluations, and routing of requests.
   • Python Service: Include a separate component for the “weight_function” directory. This service is used for computing heuristic weights and is deployed as a Firebase Function using Python.
   • Database & External Services: Depict Firebase-related resources – Firestore (with rules and indexes defined in firestore.rules and firestore.indexes.json), Firebase Authentication (with emulators configured), and potentially Firebase hosting (as configured in firebase.json and Docker info).
   • Testing & DevOps: Although not part of the production runtime, high-level testing components (Cypress, Playwright, and Jest in the tests/ and cypress/ folders) and the CI/CD workflows (GitHub workflows, Dockerfiles, and docker-compose settings) should be included to explain the development and deployment pipeline.

2. Define Relationships and Data Flows:
   • From a user’s browser (or client) a request goes to the Frontend Application.
   • The Frontend communicates with the Backend (Firebase Functions) via HTTP API calls or possibly via Firebase SDKs for authentication and Firestore access.
   • The Backend interacts with Firebase Firestore for persistent storage and possibly with Firebase Authentication for user management.
   • For specific operations — such as computing heuristic weights — the API layer routes requests to the Python-based service (weight_function) and then returns results.
   • Mark testing-related flows (e.g., end-to-end tests with Cypress, Playwright) as peripheral to indicate validation of interactions between the frontend, backend, and database.
   • Include deployment flows: Docker images are built and run, and the Firebase Emulators are used during local development.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • MVC/MVVM Pattern: The separation between Vue components (Views and Components in src) and state management via Vuex indicates a pattern where presentation and data logic are cleanly separated.
   • Serverless Backend: Firebase Functions organize the backend logic in a modular way (as seen in controllers and models).
   • Separation of Concerns: The division between the frontend (user interface), backend (API and business logic), and dedicated Python service shows clear concerns.
   • Integration with Third-Party Services: Firebase services (Firestore, Authentication, Hosting) form an integral part of the architecture.

4. Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Frontend: Vue.js 2.6.12, Vuetify 2.7.1, Vuex, and Vue Router.
   • Backend: Firebase Functions (Node.js environment), with controllers and models located in the src/controllers and src/models directories.
   • Python: A Python-based function (weight_function) to compute heuristic weights.
   • Testing: Cypress, Playwright, and Jest.
   • DevOps: Docker (Dockerfile, Dockerfile-playwright, docker-compose.yml) and CI/CD pipelines from GitHub workflows.

5. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines:
   • For a full-stack application like UX Remote LAB, clearly separate the frontend and backend layers.
   • The diagram should start with the Browser/Client invoking the Vue.js application.
   • Then, include an arrow from the frontend to the API layer (Firebase Functions), and from there to the Database (Firestore) and external authentication services.
   • Show the Python service as a microservice or an auxiliary backend component that the main API layer calls for heuristic calculations.
   • Optionally include containers or deployment environments (Docker, Firebase emulators) in a side box to illustrate the operational environment.

6. Diagram Elements and Visual Guidelines:
   • Use clear, legible labels for each major component (e.g., “Vue Frontend,” “Firebase Functions API,” “Firestore Database,” “Python Heuristic Service”).
   • Draw directional arrows to illustrate data flow:
     – User actions (requests) flow from Browser → Vue Frontend.
     – Vue Frontend communicates with Firebase Functions (API calls).
     – Firebase Functions interact with Firestore and, when needed, call the Python service.
   • Apply different shapes or colors to distinguish component types:
     – Rectangles for frontend UI components.
     – Cylinders for databases (Firestore).
     – Rounded boxes for serverless functions and microservices.
     – Dashed lines might be used for development/testing flows (e.g., CI/CD pipelines, Firebase Emulators).
   • Consider adding a legend in the diagram to describe the icons or color codes you use.

7. Additional Details:
   • Emphasize environmental configuration aspects (like .env for Firebase configuration) in a brief side-note.
   • Optionally illustrate that the project supports local emulation with Firebase Emulators and Docker setups for deployment.
   • Ensure that even auxiliary components (such as testing scripts in Cypress and GitHub workflows) are represented or annotated, as they provide insight into the development lifecycle.

By following these guidelines, you will produce a highly detailed system design diagram that accurately captures the core architectural elements and interactions of UX Remote LAB, ensuring clarity for any principal software engineer reviewing the system's architecture.
</explanation>
